idiom_name: AnyIterator { next element or nil } / sequence(first:next:)
implementation_notes: Swift supplies generators as standard-library types rather than a language statement: AnyIterator wraps a closure returning the next element (nil ends the sequence), sequence(first:next:) and sequence(state:next:) build lazy sequences from a seed, and a custom type conforms to Sequence by returning an IteratorProtocol from makeIterator(). for-in drives any of them and stops calling next() when the loop exits, so the producer simply stops; the closure forms keep the state explicit and are the shortest path from an algorithm to a lazy source.
code_sketch:
var state = 0
let counter = AnyIterator { () -> Int? in
    defer { state += 1 }               // explicit producer state
    return state < 3 ? state : nil     // nil ends the sequence
}

for value in counter { print(value) }  // 0 1 2, then done
pitfalls: AnyIterator is a single-pass iterator, not a collection: iterating the same value twice continues from where it stopped, so return a fresh iterator (or a Sequence whose makeIterator() builds one) when replayability matters.

The closure runs synchronously per element on the caller's thread: blocking work inside it blocks the loop, and a closure that never returns (or a for-in with no exit) hangs with no compiler warning; unbounded sequences need take/prefix or an explicit bound.

variants.name: AsyncStream / AsyncSequence (for await)
variants.idiom_name: AsyncStream { continuation in ... } with for await and onTermination
variants.implementation_notes: Since Swift 5.5 a generator can be asynchronous: AsyncStream { continuation in ... } (or a custom AsyncSequence) yields elements with continuation.yield(...) and finishes with finish(), consumers write for await element in stream, and task cancellation is delivered through onTermination. Use it when elements are produced by awaiting I/O or by another task, and remember that the continuation is owned by the producer: cleanup (cancelling the task, closing the file) belongs in onTermination, because the loop's break only ends consumption.
pitfalls: AsyncStream buffers by default: a producer that outruns the consumer grows the buffer unless the buffering policy is set to .bufferingNewest/.bufferingOldest or the loop applies backpressure - memory grows silently otherwise.

The continuation must be finished exactly once and only after production stops: yielding after finish() is a no-op, and dropping the continuation without finish() leaves for-await loops suspended forever.
